opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift for me was realizing that being a CEO is very different from being an engineer or a researcher. When I was working on Taichi during my PhD, my job was basically to write good code and solve hard technical problems myself. As a CEO, my job is to build the system that solves the problems, and that system is mostly people.

So I often think of the role in a few layers. First, the CEO sets the direction: what we're building, for whom, and why now. In AI especially, things move incredibly fast. A model that was state of the art six months ago might be ordinary today. So a big part of my job is making sure we're pointed at the right problem and not just chasing whatever is hot.

Second, the CEO is responsible for the team: hiring great people, giving them context, and then getting out of their way. Early on I had a tendency to want to do everything myself, because as an engineer that's what you're trained to do. But that doesn't scale. If I'm the bottleneck on every decision, the company can only move as fast as I can. So I try to give people ownership and focus my energy on the few decisions only I can make.

Third, and people don't talk about this as much, the CEO makes sure the company doesn't die. That means watching cash, fundraising, and making the hard calls when something isn't working. Not the most exciting part, but if you don't do it, nothing else matters.

And I'd add one more thing: the CEO has to be the person who cares most about the users. Engineers can fall in love with technology. I'm guilty of that too. But at the end of the day, a company exists because it creates value for people. So I spend a lot of time talking to users, reading feedback, trying to understand what they actually need, not what I think is cool.

Honestly, I'm still learning. I don't think anyone is born knowing how to be a CEO. You learn by making mistakes, hopefully small ones, and adjusting quickly. In that way it's not so different from research: you form a hypothesis, test it, and iterate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting from individual technical work to building a system of people, but does not say the CEO must periodically “fire themselves.”

r002.rationale: It describes setting direction and making hard calls, but does not state that the CEO should put the whole company’s interests ahead of being liked by everyone.

r003.rationale: It compares learning to be a CEO with research and iteration, but does not call starting a business the best form of personal training in peacetime.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't start out thinking of myself as a CEO at all. I was a PhD student at MIT writing a programming language, Taichi, because I was frustrated with how hard it was to write high-performance graphics and simulation code. I thought of myself as a researcher and a programmer. The company came later, and the title came with it.

So the way I think about the role now is that my job is to make the best decisions for the company, not to be the best engineer in the company. That was a hard shift for me. In the early days I was still writing a lot of code, and I enjoyed it, but at some point I realized that if I'm the one deciding what gets built, where we spend money, and who we hire, then every hour I spend fixing a compiler bug is an hour I'm not spending on the problems that only I can own. The team is full of excellent engineers. There isn't anyone else who can set direction.

The second thing is that I try to be very honest with myself about what I don't know. I came from an academic background, so things like go-to-market, pricing, sales, managing a budget, these were all new to me. I think the worst thing a technical founder can do is pretend that because they're good at one hard thing, they'll naturally be good at every hard thing. I read a lot, I talk to people who have done it before, and I try to hire people who are better than me in those areas and then actually listen to them.

The third piece is culture. When you're small, the way you behave becomes the way the company behaves. If I cut corners, people will cut corners. If I'm transparent about the hard decisions and why we made them, people will trust the process even when they disagree with the outcome. So I spend more time than I expected on communication, on explaining the reasoning, not just the conclusion.

And finally, I try to stay close to the product and the users. Taichi started as an open-source project, and that community is a big part of why the company exists. I still read GitHub issues, I still go on the forum. It keeps me grounded in what people actually need rather than what I imagine they need. I think a CEO who loses touch with the product ends up optimizing for the wrong things.

So in short: own the decisions, be honest about your gaps, set the culture through your own behavior, and never get too far from the users. It's a very different job from research, but I've come to enjoy it in its own way.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifting from engineering to company-wide decisions, but never says a CEO must periodically “fire themselves.”

r002.rationale: The response says the CEO should make the best decisions for the company, but does not address prioritizing company interests over being liked by everyone.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize starting a business as the best form of personal training available in peacetime.

astra-6.text:
I think of the CEO role as doing whatever the company needs most at that moment. My background is technical, so my instinct is to work on the technology. But being CEO means asking a different question: Is that actually the most important thing I can do today? Sometimes it is. Other times, it’s talking to customers, recruiting someone, or making sure the team understands what we’re trying to achieve.

You also have to connect the long-term vision with the next concrete step. You can have an ambitious idea, but you still need to figure out who needs the product, what problem it solves for them, and what we should build first. For me, that means being willing to learn and change what I do as the company grows.

r001.rationale: The response says the CEO should adapt their work as the company grows, but it does not describe periodically “firing themselves.”

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing the company’s most important needs, but does not say to prioritize the company over being liked by everyone.

r003.rationale: The response does not judge starting a business as the best form of personal training in peacetime.

sol-6.1.text: I think my role as CEO is to figure out what matters most for the company and then make sure we can actually do it. That means setting a direction, bringing together the right people, and helping them work well together. My background is technical, so it’s tempting to spend all my time on the technology. But building a company requires a broader perspective: Are we solving a real problem for customers? Can we turn the technology into something people find useful? I’m still learning how to balance those responsibilities, and where I can contribute the most as the company grows.
